newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish secularists gloat over Erbakan resignation.
newsitem.headline: Turkish secularists gloat over Erbakan resignation.

text.p: Turkish secularists gloated on Wednesday at the resignation of Necmettin Erbakan, who quit as prime minister under secularist pressure after a year as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.

"To hell with him, we've had enough, we don't want Erbakan or any of his lot any more. I just hope we've seen the last of them that's all," said Zeynep Peker in Nisantasi, an posh upmarket Istanbul district famed for expensive boutiques.
Erbakan handed in his resignation to President Suleyman Demirel on Wednesday evening as part of a bid to form a caretaker government, led by his pro-Western deputy Tansu Ciller into early elections.

The plan, first unveiled at the start of June, is designed to head off an assault by Turkey's powerful military, angered at Erbakan's failure to stem an alleged rise in Islamist activism since he came to power.

"All they have done in the last year is strengthen religious reaction and fill government offices with their own people," said Bilge Bilgic, head of the Ataturk Philosophy Association, which seeks to defend the legacy of Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk.

Many Turks in Istanbul's upmarket malls and shopping streets were angry at efforts by Erbakan's Welfare Party to bring an Islamic atmosphere into public life with plans for mosques in secular strongholds and encouragement of religous brotherhoods.
Welfare gained power after narrowly winning 21 percent of the vote at 1995 general elections.
Secularists saw his vision of global Moslem brotherhood as an attempt to undermine the republic forged by Ataturk from the remnants of the Ottoman Empire, run along Islamic lines.
"They want to drag us back to the middle ages, to turn the country into an Iran, or Saudi Arabia," said Hasan, drinking beer next to the Bosphorus Straits in Istanbul's trendy Ortakoy.
Erbakan visited Iran and Libya shortly after taking power, causing outrage in the mainstream media, which mounted an often ferocious campaign against his rule.

"Erbakan came to power declaring a just order... He could only manage one year as prime minister...Erbakan had to hand over the premiership to avoid his party being closed down," the mass-circulation daily Sabah declared in its front page on Wednesday in anticipation of the resignation .
The 70-year old Erbakan for his part, accused the media barons of creating a "false agenda" which dogged his every step and did nothing but create tension.

Turkey's military, self-declared guardians of the secular order, ordered a series anti-Islamist measures in February which slowly undermined Erbakan's unlikely coalition with Ciller's secularist True Path Party.
Erbakan stalled on implementing the measures and the army, which has staged three coups since 1960, declared it would use "force of arms" if necessary to defend the secular order.
Defections from the government and an ultimatum from True Path, finally forced Erbakan to resign and try to save the coalition under Ciller's leadership.
"If you ask me, it's great, God saved us from him," said Kaan Hamacioglu, a nightclub DJ.
The proposed transfer of power still faces a host of procedural and political obstacles. It is not certain whether Ciller or any of the opposition leaders will be able to form a fresh coalition.
"I'm glad he's going, but whoever it is that comes in his place, all they care about is how to rip the country off," said Mahmut Demir, surveying the traffic from behind the wheel of his taxi.
